Olha... é clássico. Mas clássico ≠ perfeito. Pânico inventou a regra de "não transar, não beber, não falar 'vou já volto'". Ok, genial pra 1996. O problema é que 6 filmes depois a franquia ainda tá jogando o mesmo jogo. O terror é meio básico. Ghostface aparece, dá umas facadas, solta uma piada metalinguística, e 20 min depois tem outro diálogo explicando as "regras do terror". De novo. Pelo 5º filme seguido. Os sustos são jumpscare de som alto. O mistério do assassino é sempre "alguém que você viu 2 vezes no filme". E o massacre no ensino médio virou fórmula de fast-food. Sim, satirizou os slashers e salvou o gênero nos anos 90. Mérito total. Mas hoje assistir Pânico dá uma preguiça. Porque é sempre Woodsboro, sempre a Sidney chorando, sempre o mesmo roteiro com roupa nova e elenco mais jovem. Não merece 1/4 da fama que tem. Virou "terror pra quem não gosta de terror". É confortável, é meme, é nostálgico. Mas assustar mesmo? Já não assusta. "Não é sobre QUEM, é sobre POR QUÊ." Pois é. E o "porquê" depois do 3º filme já enjoa. Respeito a história. So, after years of resolutely talking shit, I decided to give Scream another try. Wes Craven's fourth most interesting meta horror film is almost universally beloved but, personally, I don't really see what the fuss is about. Still carrying the stink of Vampire in Brooklyn, Craven beats Joss Whedon to the punch for the obnoxious elder millennial teen banter (I can say it, I was the target audience) but the entire exercise feels, well, about as hokey and forced as Eddie Murphy trying to be a funny vampire. The self-awareness might have been impressive if Craven hadn't landed the one-two punch of Shocker and New Nightmare just a few years earlier. Shocker does all the same self-referential humor that Scream does but shows up with not only a real mean streak but also a complete lack of restraint. New Nightmare tackles the deconstruction of a genre Craven helped solidify with more  intelligence and genuine terror than Scream even hints at. It all feels like we've seen it before but Craven has decided to dumb it down for the folks in the back. Scream isn't helped by a wildly uneven cast. Drew Barrymore's opening scene is the highpoint of the film and sets a bar that nothing else in Scream even brushes against. Rose McGowan probably comes closest but an underwritten role does her no favors. Though Neve Campbell is perfectly sufficient as a final girl, she suffers from being given too little to upend in a movie thats supposed to be about upending expectations. Unfortunately, the good news ends there. David Arquette, who I have a genuine soft spot for, wanders in and out of frame uselessly as he's circled by Courtney Cox, whose intentions are vague. The always execrable Matthew Lillard and a Johnny Depp lookalike named "Skeet" fail to either smolder or clown effectively, with Skeet in particular seeming to be completely incapable of maintaining the mystery. I can't call Scream a bad film, its competent enough, but theres a bloodlessness and slick presentation that is a far way off from the guy who made you need a shower after Last House on the Left. It is, well and truly, just ok. It made him a bunch of money, though, and Wes deserved that. Level of concern your friends will have when you recommend this movie: low.

Trying to write my thoughts down on Scream as someone who's only seen a handful of iconic horror films feels like a losing game. It's so baked in irony and endless references to other films, most of which I was completely unfamiliar with, to the point where it got increasingly frustrating over time. I felt like I was thinking too hard about i for most of its runtime instead of appreciating it, which tends to be a bad sign when it comes to comedy. To give credit where it's due, the opening scene is absolutely insane and one of the few times I really understood why everyone loves this thing...it has everything you need for an effective horror cold open. Unfortunately, it's also one of the few times I felt like the film actually scared me. Admittedly, the whole film feels like a big joke I'm not in on, which is why it doesn't really work as a comedy. Meta movies like this are why I always pegged myself as not a horror guy; even when it's embraced as thoroughly as it is here, the tropes present still grind my gears a good bit. On the bright side, the deaths tend to be gnarly and the characters are likable enough every now and then that they can evoke a few laughs from my cold, charred heart. Two films in and it's a bit hard to tell what I think of Wes Craven so far. Red Eye wasn't a masterpiece by any means, but it was an entertaining and light thriller aware of its limitations with some great performances from Rachel McAdams, Cillian Murphy and Brian Cox. I can see why Neve Campbell and Matthew Lillard went on to become iconic actors, even if I wasn't wowed by them here. It's a bit disappointing for me to not fall in love with the first horror movie I watch from such an iconic horror director, but I think I need to familiarize myself with more slashers and Craven's initial run of films to appreciate this one more. Need more self-aware horror like the original Funny Games (which was also way funnier!) and less like this.

Scream is one of those landmark moments in movies where there's pre-Scream slashers and there's post-Scream slashers. The way it laid bare the common horror tropes is something we take for granted these days; the whole "How to Survive a Horror Movie" started right here. It was incredibly clever and fresh for its time, but that subversive nature has been over-done so much throughout the years that watching it now feels downright bland. This movie's biggest sin is the annoying thing movies do where it points out that something is cliché or stupid but then also does it; as if pointing it out makes it better. That's kinda this whole franchise's conceit; being a slasher while commenting on itself. I do have to point out that seeing Scary Movie a lot has made a lot of moments here incredibly laughable and I can't help but think about the goofy parody parts instead of the serious ones. Dewey for instance is so inept, he might as well be the Doofy character from SM. I suppose this could be seen as an indictment of disturbed, privileged, horror movie-obsessed young white men, but that same obsession can also be seen as a saving grace so the message is a little muddy there. An element I do enjoy is that this makes the effort to show that Ghostface is definitely human and that victims who fight back do cause harm. I also liked the double-meta bit of Randy telling Jamie Lee Curtis on the TV to turn around while the killer is behind him; him saying "Behind you, Jamie" is Randy also talking to his actor self Jamie Kennedy, clever stuff. Overall important for horror history, but these days it kinda falls into the same horror heap it was trying to satire.

scream permanece como um filme fundamental, mas sua consagração também criou uma espécie de blindagem crítica que transforma qualquer ressalva em heresia: basta mencionar que o roteiro é mais inteligente do que propriamente profundo, que os diálogos frequentemente confundem autoconsciência com esperteza ou que a revelação de billy loomis e stu macher é menos perturbadora do que o mito em torno dela para que a obra seja imediatamente defendida como uma perfeição intocável. wes craven e kevin williamson revitalizaram o slasher ao fazer seus personagens conhecerem as regras do gênero e ao transformar o repertório do público em instrumento de suspense, mas essa inovação não deve ser confundida com uma reinvenção absoluta do horror: scream é, sobretudo, uma síntese extremamente eficiente de ideias anteriores, uma obra que desmonta os clichês enquanto ainda depende deles para existir. sua inteligência está na forma, no ritmo, na mise-en-scène e na habilidade de fazer a expectativa do espectador trabalhar contra si mesma, não necessariamente na profundidade de suas conclusões. a abertura com casey becker continua sendo uma aula de construção de tensão, porque craven entende que o terror não nasce apenas da violência, mas da transformação gradual de uma conversa banal em um jogo de humilhação, controle e morte; depois disso, porém, o filme nem sempre sustenta a mesma precisão, alternando momentos de genuína ameaça com diálogos que soam excessivamente artificiais, como se os personagens estivessem mais interessados em demonstrar conhecimento sobre filmes de terror do que em existir dentro daquele mundo. sidney prescott é uma protagonista importante e muito bem defendida por neve campbell, mas sua trajetória ainda parte de um modelo recorrente do slasher: a jovem marcada pelo trauma materno, perseguida por uma violência que invade sua sexualidade, sua casa e sua relação amorosa. o que torna sidney mais complexa é justamente a descoberta de que o perigo não vem de um monstro distante, mas do namorado, do amigo e do ambiente masculino que parecia familiar; billy e stu não são os melhores assassinos da franquia, e suas motivações, quando finalmente expostas, parecem apressadas, superficiais e dramaticamente menores do que a tensão construída ao longo do filme. a ideia de que billy matou maureen prescott por ressentimento e que stu simplesmente o acompanha por uma combinação de instabilidade e submissão é funcional, mas não possui a dimensão psicológica que muitos fãs projetam sobre a dupla; a revelação é mais memorável pela encenação e pelo impacto histórico do que pela riqueza do texto. ainda assim, há algo profundamente perturbador na escolha de colocar a violência nas mãos de dois garotos comuns, e não de uma figura sobrenatural ou de um assassino fisicamente invencível: ghostface é icônico porque não é uma identidade estável, mas uma máscara que permite ao homem comum transformar misoginia, sadismo e desejo de controle em espetáculo. sob o humor, a metalinguagem e as referências aos clássicos, scream também revela como a cultura cinematográfica masculina frequentemente converte a violência contra mulheres em entretenimento, debate e trivia, enquanto as próprias vítimas precisam aprender as regras de um jogo criado para matá-las. o filme percebe essa contradição, mas nem sempre a enfrenta com a mesma contundência com que a apresenta; muitas vezes, sua crítica ao gênero é absorvida pelo prazer de reproduzir o que pretende questionar. visualmente, entretanto, a obra permanece extraordinariamente segura: a fotografia noturna, os interiores domésticos, a paleta fria e a arquitetura isolada de woodsboro criam um espaço onde a adolescência parece simultaneamente cotidiana e teatral, como se cada corredor pudesse se transformar em cenário de uma performance homicida. a trilha, a montagem e a direção de craven sustentam um equilíbrio raro entre humor, tensão e violência, embora o filme esteja longe de ser tão assustador quanto sua reputação sugere; ele intriga mais do que apavora, diverte mais do que assombra e permanece na memória mais pela sua personalidade do que pela capacidade de provocar medo genuíno. como grande fã da franquia, reconheço sua importância, amo ghostface e compreendo por que scream se tornou uma referência incontornável do horror, mas justamente por amá-lo não vejo necessidade de tratá-lo como uma obra perfeita: sua relevância histórica é maior do que sua consistência dramática, sua influência é mais revolucionária do que seu argumento e seu legado acabou sendo fortalecido por sequências que ampliaram, corrigiram e até superaram aspectos de sua fórmula original. scream continua sendo um filme excelente, carismático e decisivo para o slasher moderno, mas envelheceu menos como vinho do que como um retrato muito bem preservado de seu próprio momento, brilhante na autoconsciência, irregular na dramaturgia e muito mais desafiador do que assustador.

In my opinion, Scream, released in 1996 and directed by Wes Craven, is a very interesting horror movie that combines suspense, violence, mystery, and some moments of humor. The movie tells the story of Sidney Prescott, a young woman who is being chased by a mysterious killer who wears a mask and calls his victims before attacking them. What I liked most about the movie is the way it creates tension. From the beginning, the viewer has the feeling that any character could become the next victim. The phone calls from the killer make the story even more suspenseful because he talks to his victims and plays with them before attacking. I also liked the way Scream uses the horror genre. It is not just a movie with scary and violent scenes. It also makes references to other horror movies and plays with some of the common rules of the genre. This makes the story different from other slasher movies and makes the viewer try to discover who the killer is. Another positive point is the characters, especially Sidney. Throughout the movie, she becomes stronger and more confident while facing difficult situations. The actors also help make the scenes feel more realistic and create a strong sense of fear and suspense. The killer's mask is another memorable part of the movie because it looks simple but is also very frightening. Even though I really enjoyed the movie, some parts can be predictable for people who are already familiar with horror movies. However, this does not completely take away from the suspense because the movie keeps the mystery about who is behind the mask until the end. Overall, I think Scream is a very interesting horror and suspense movie. I liked the way it combines the slasher style with mystery and humor. For me, it is a movie that keeps the viewer interested from beginning to end and shows why Scream became an important movie in the horror genre.

Scream is the ultimate love letter to the slasher genre. It’s more than just a laundry list of references and tropes, it provides smart, self aware commentary on the genre while bringing it back to some of its earliest roots in a classic whodunnit. There’s nothing I can add to reviewing the intro, it’s legendary. It does rely a little on the audience knowing Barrymore’s star power in the 90s, but largely still works without that prior knowledge. One of my favorite aspects of this film is its score. It’s heavy. It forces mood down your throat. It’s awesome. On the subject of sound, the moves sound design does include some fairly campy stock sound effects. They’re goofy but don’t detract too much. They also work well with the perpetual clumsiness of Ghostface. To me they also serve as a nice node to general campiness of slasher’s past. The plot is cool for a slasher, as it brings you back to whodunnits that predate slashers, and were a prevalent aspect of some early ones. The movie does a pretty clever job of keeping you guessing who the killer is. Every time you think you have it nailed down, something detracts you.

“What's your favorite scary movie?” Randy was so right and now that I rewatched this movie three times: you could clearly guess who were the killers from the beginning, at least for Billy. It was so obvious and also not so obvious. I loved both Stu and Billy’s acting (same for the other actors), but damn, Matthew Lillard and Skeet Ulrich put up with an amazing performance here. I have so much to tell about that movie but I’ll be short. This is the kind of movies I could rewatch again and again and would never get bored of. I think that’d be called a comfort movie, although Scream isn’t exactly the type of movie that makes you want to smile or laugh. But Scream , after rewatching it, is like predicting everything that will happen. We know who the killers are, we know who are going to die or not and yet, we don’t care. There are no surprises, but this feels comfortable. In a way, that is what makes horror movies comforting (in my opinion). I rate it as a 5* now because somewhere in my heart, Scream deserves it in every way.
